title: Our one rule for AI code is that it isn't allowed to guess. What worked and what didn't on our card roguelite (team of 3)
author: Jeffonious
selftext:
Since July, three of us have been making a card roguelite called Grim Gambit, where every card you put down is a higher-or-lower bet. Most of the code was written with AI coding tools, and a large chunk of that was done with local LLMs running on our own machines. Most of the art is AI-generated too, with PixelLab. The game design, the writing and every decision about what makes it in are ours. Here's what has held up for us and what hasn't.



The biggest thing was writing the rules of the game down in one big document and telling the AI it isn't allowed to guess. If the document doesn't cover what it's about to build, it has to stop and ask us. Every time we make a design call, it goes into that document with a date on it. It's huge now, but when something in the game acts weird we can go look up what it was supposed to do. Either the code got it wrong or we did, and it's usually easy to tell which.



The second thing was keeping the game's rules separate from everything you see on screen. That means what the AI writes for the rules can be tested automatically, without anyone clicking through the game. It also means we can have a bot play game after game on its own, counting cards the whole time. So when one of us says "this character feels too hard early on", we don't argue about it, we go check. One character turned out to be losing 26% of first runs on the smallest board, compared to 16% with no character at all, so we moved her later in the unlock order.



For art, the lesson was that describing a style to an AI doesn't hold up for long. What worked was measuring the art we already had (how bright it is, how colorful, how much black is in it) and checking every new piece against those numbers. We also never take the first thing it makes. It makes a batch of cheap options, drops each one into an actual screenshot of the game, and one of us picks. And we keep a log of the prompt and settings for everything, so we can make it again or match it later.



# Stuff that didn't work. 

Props generated on their own and placed on a painted background looked like stickers. We had to fade them back and dull the colors before they looked like they belonged.



We tried animating little details on the weapons and the blades turned into brown blobs every single time, so we gave up on that. Anything we had the AI draw with code, like a candle and a lantern, looked wrong next to everything else. And in our experience AI is bad at judging its own art. We had it score a set of backgrounds once, and the one we all liked best came in last.



I'm curious how other people here keep a consistent look across hundreds of pieces. We have generation guidelines and agents review each asset, but art consistency is the largest time constraint.  Is there anything better than "measure it and have a person pick"?



If you want to see how it turned out, there's a free demo that runs in a desktop browser:[ \[Grim Gambit demo\]](https://grimgambit.reignofgaming.gg/?src=reddit-aigamedev).   
  
The Steam page is[ \[here\]](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5009760/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=aigamedev).

comments.body:
Love to see responsible AI usage that helps developers and not simply "an AI made this game".

Looks great so far!
